title: First West Coast engagement and Stormy Weather
summary: At Billy Berg's Swing Club in Hollywood his band stayed eight weeks, and Mike Gould offered him arranging work on Stormy Weather.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Right. Okay. Now let's approach the Hollywood days as you go on tour in 1942, you play in 1943, and you arrive in California -- you don't go to

California, as I understand it, to go to Hollywood, particularly, with an idea of writing for films, but rather, you're taking your band out on a normal tour and you wind up playing on the West Coast, as well as between the two coasts along the way and your first engagement, as you recall it, on the West Coast in the Los Angeles area took place when and where? Do you recall that?
Oh yes. We were billed to go in to -- or booked to go in to a club called the Swing Club.
Uh huh.

And that was on Las Palmas Avenue at Hollywood Boulevard. Actually, a little bit north of Hollywood Boulevard. Run by a man named Billy Berg. My manager at that time was Carlos Castell, who was also the manager of Stan Kenton, and I believe, Sonny Dunham's orchestra --and we went in to this club -- I think we were booked in for 2 weeks, and it seems to me we stayed 8; did tremendous business there, and during the time I was there, they were making a film at 20th Century Fox called "Stormy Weather."
Right.

And I was contacted by my friend Mike Gould who was at the time working with Irving Mills, who was one of the producers of the picture, and I was asked if I would like to do some arranging on the picture.
And I accepted, and that was the first work that
was the first work that I did on a Hollywood film.
So this was probably the summer of '43 or roughly in there, or the Fall?
Yeah, about the summer, maybe. Yes.
And that's the first time that you worked regularly with Fats Waller on a project?
Yes, yes. He was in the picture.
Right. And did you appear in that film on screen?
No, I didn't.
You played?
I played on the soundtrack.
Right. And some of those were issued as records later on?
Yes.
But officially, they were not pirated.
So this was the first arranging you did in Hollywood, in the summer or late in 1943, a little bit ...
